# The two invariances ISLA is built for {#sec-invariances}

**ISLA is built around two facts that every boundary-driven PDE respects: the answer does not depend on where the body
sits or how it is turned, and it does not depend on how the boundary was meshed.** The first fact gives an exact contract,
rigid-motion equivariance, which ISLA holds to roundoff. The second gives a convergence property, discretization
consistency, which ISLA holds in the fine-mesh limit and which decides whether a change to the architecture is adopted. This chapter states both as exact tests on the code. It then says what each one buys, draws the sampling
laws through which the second is measured, and reads both off the standing of the three reference configurations on every
dataset. It closes with what still moves ISLA's own error: the other prediction points of a request (interacting ISLA's; ISLA-DTT,
the default interior form, is independent of them), a token budget below
the boundary's resolution, a different surface, and float32 ties in the geometry.

*Before this chapter:* @sec-isla (tokens, measure weights, the length unit $L$, slices and anchors, relational invariants,
the equivariant heads) and @sec-metrics (the area-weighted relative L2 error). The scoring protocol is @sec-protocol.

```{python}
#| label: setup-invariances
#| include: false
```

## Two of the four properties need work {#sec-four-properties}

**A surrogate for a boundary-driven PDE should have four properties, and two of them come with any slice-attention
model.** *Global interaction*, every boundary patch able to influence every output, holds for ISLA, GeoTransolver and
Transolver alike: their routing runs over the whole boundary with no neighborhoods or cutoffs. *Units invariance* comes from
nondimensionalizing inputs and targets, which every pipeline in this book does. The other two need a construction.
*Rigid-motion equivariance* is exact for ISLA: a test on the code passes to roundoff in float64. *Discretization
consistency* is a convergence property: it is measured, and it decides whether a change to the architecture is adopted
(@sec-principle).

## The contracts, as tests {#sec-isla-contracts}

**Each contract is a property of the code, checked in double precision on random weights and a random point cloud. A
trained checkpoint cannot break it.** The fixture of `test/experimental/models/isla/test_isla.py` is an ISLA with width
64, 3 layers and 32 slices, in float64, on 500 boundary cells. The cells have random normals and random measure weights, and
the cloud is stretched by 3:2:1 along its axes, so no rotation leaves it unchanged. The model declares one scalar output
$p$, one vector output $v$ and one global direction $\hat g$. A test transforms the input, runs the model, and compares the
output with the transformed output of the untransformed input. @tbl-contracts lists the tests by the transformation they
apply.

| transformation of the input | what must hold | tolerance |
|---|---|---:|
| rotation $x \mapsto Qx$, $\det Q = 1$; normals and $\hat g$ rotated with it | $p$ unchanged, $v \mapsto Qv$ | $10^{-10}$ |
| reflection, $\det Q = -1$ | a rank-$r$ output of even parity maps as $Q^{\otimes r}$; an odd-parity output (a pseudotensor) also picks up $\det Q$ | $10^{-11}$; $10^{-4}$ relative in two dimensions |
| translation $x \mapsto x + t$ | every output unchanged, with no centering in the learned path | $10^{-10}$ |
| uniform rescale $x \mapsto kx$, measures $\times k^2$ or left alone | every output unchanged, with prediction points moved along | $10^{-10}$ |
| measure-weight rescale $w \mapsto 137\,w$ | every output unchanged: the routing reads $\log w$ through a softmax, which a constant shift does not move | $10^{-9}$ |
| cell splitting: every cell replaced by two coincident copies of half its measure | the interior prediction unchanged: the discrete measure, and every integral over it, is the same | $10^{-10}$ |
| refinement of a fractal boundary (Koch curve, total length $\to \infty$) | the length unit $L$ converges: successive levels agree to $10^{-3}$ from level 4 on | converges |
| a 10:1 biased resampling of 100,000 cells to 10,000, with Horvitz–Thompson weights | the prediction moves by less than four times what a fresh uniform draw moves it | ratio $< 4$ |
| boundary conditions: the cells of one condition permuted; the input mapping given in another order | the outputs permute with the cells; the outputs unchanged, bitwise | $10^{-10}$; bitwise |
| one condition remeshed by cell splitting, each condition in turn | the interior prediction unchanged | $10^{-10}$ |
| a prediction point's wall distance and direction under another draw of the boundary tokens, and under splitting the surface's cells | unchanged: they are functions of the full-resolution surface | bitwise; $10^{-12}$ |
| a prediction point moved through the surface | its distance channels and direction continuous | continuous |

: The contract tests and what each verifies. The transformations act on the boundary cells (positions, normals, measure
weights), on the global directions and, for the interior task, on the prediction points together. How to read this: a
tolerance is an absolute bound on the output difference in float64, except the two-dimensional test, which runs in float32
at a relative tolerance of $10^{-4}$; a contract that holds here holds for every set of weights, trained or not. ISLA-DTT's forest read keeps the rotation and translation rows at its working opening angle; where the
frame the forest is built in ties, a rigid motion regroups clusters and moves the read only by the tree's error, which
vanishes as $\theta \to 0$. In the code as it is, rounding
decides the sign octant of most of the lug's cells and many exact ties of the forest's box test, so on the lug
a rigid motion changes the forest, and ISLA-DTT's posed error is not its native one (@sec-arch-tree-read). The test functions are listed below. Source:
`test/experimental/models/isla/`.
{#tbl-contracts tbl-colwidths="[36,50,14]"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional: the test functions, row by row"}
Rotation: `test_rotation_equivariance`, `test_frame_contracts` (`test_isla.py`). Reflection:
`test_covariance_of_every_rank_and_parity` (`test_isla_heads.py`), `test_boundary_inputs_covariance`
(`test_isla_inputs.py`), and the two-dimensional
`test_two_dimensional_contracts_rotation_translation_magnitude_and_reflection` (`test_isla_nd.py`). Translation:
`test_translation_invariance`, `test_translation_invariance_alone`. Uniform rescale: `test_geometric_scale_equivariance`,
`test_rms_distance_scale_contracts`. Measure-weight rescale: `test_measure_scale_invariance`. Cell splitting:
`test_query_mass_refinement_invariance`. Refinement:
`test_rms_distance_converges_on_koch_curve_where_total_measure_diverges`. Biased resampling:
`test_frame_is_sampling_consistent`. Boundary conditions: `test_a_condition_s_cells_permute_with_its_outputs`,
`test_the_order_of_the_input_mapping_changes_nothing`, `test_remeshing_one_condition_changes_no_interior_prediction` and
`test_every_condition_s_fields_are_covariant` (`test_isla_conditions.py`). The prediction points' geometry:
`test_builtin_geometry_is_the_surface_s_for_every_draw_of_the_tokens`, `test_exact_geometry_is_invariant_to_splitting_the_surface`,
`test_exact_geometry_is_covariant_and_scales`, `test_convergence_is_second_order_under_refinement`
(`test_isla_interior_geometry.py`) and `test_query_encoding_is_continuous_at_the_surface` (`test_isla_query_encoding.py`). The

:::

The first five rows are exact symmetries of the algebra. Positions enter only as differences to slice anchors, which are
themselves measure-weighted means. The length unit $L$, the measure-weighted RMS pairwise distance of the full-resolution boundary, is
an integral that scales with the geometry. Every scalar the network forms is a norm or an inner product of vectors that
rotate together (@sec-isla-frame, @sec-isla-relational). Vector and tensor outputs are assembled in a basis built from those
same vectors (@sec-isla-heads). The last three rows are discretization statements. Cell splitting is exact, because a
quadrature over the split cells is the same sum. Refinement and resampling are statements about a limit, and the next two
sections are about them.

**On the interior task the boundary draw is pose-invariant in the limit of its token budget.** A boundary with more cells
than the budget `boundary_tokens` is subsampled by the systematic draw of @sec-arch-boundary-draw, which lays the cells
along a Morton order of their centroids taken in the boundary's canonical frame. The frame turns with the body, so a rotated
case draws the same cells except where float32 rounding of its coordinates moves a centroid across a grid line of the Morton
code, or where the boundary's principal moments nearly tie and the frame itself turns; there its prediction moves by the
difference between two quadratures of the same surface. That difference vanishes as the budget
reaches the full resolution, where every cell is kept, and the posed protocol measures what remains at the working budget;
the standings' posed numbers were measured with a draw ordered along the dataset's axes (@sec-standing-geometry), under
which a pose changes many of the drawn cells of a subsampled boundary (@sec-medial-ties).
A boundary with no more cells than the budget is kept whole and is exact, as in the tests above. The length unit, the
declared scales and each prediction point's wall geometry are computed from the full-resolution boundary before the draw,
so none of them moves with it.

::: {.callout-warning title="What is not a contract"}
- **The magnitude of a global vector input.** It is discarded by design: a direction is normalized, and a magnitude that
  matters (a speed, a Reynolds number) enters as a global scalar.
- **Independence from the other prediction points.** In ISLA's interacting interior form, every prediction point is a token
  that writes into the slices, so a prediction depends on which other points are in the request
  (@sec-query-population measures it). ISLA-DTT
  (`query_independent=True`) makes its prediction points read-only, and its independence is a contract
  (`test_query_independent_interior_contracts`; @sec-arch-modes).
- **Completeness of the representation.** The anchors are first moments, so two arrangements with the same first moments
  per slice are indistinguishable to a layer (`results/isla_first_moment_collision_2026-09-08.json`).
- **The deployed arithmetic.** The tests run in float64. On the GPU in float32 the algebra keeps the contract to float32
  roundoff, but the geometry of the interior task has two discrete steps that roundoff can still decide: which features
  join the tie set of a point equally far from two, and which cells the token draw keeps under a pose (@sec-medial-ties).
  The standings' checkpoints were trained with a geometry in which roundoff also picked the tied feature and the sign of
  the distance at a fold of the surface, and the token draw followed the dataset's axes (@sec-standing-geometry). ISLA's rotated-and-translated error stays within
  `{python} f"{POSED_DEV:.1%}"` of its native error on every headline field of every task with a final
  `{python} Markdown(f"standing{EXCEPT_TXT} (@tbl-contract-shifts). {S.tally_note()}")` On HiLiftAeroML, a surface task, it is
  `{python} f"{ST['hilift'].shift('ISLA', HEAD['hilift'], 'posed'):.3f}"` times native, outside the 0.2% registered for it;
  what produces that move is not located (@sec-de-limits). Under *bfloat16 autocast* (matrix products
  run in the 16-bit bfloat16 format, with an 8-bit significand of which 7 bits are stored) the rounding is larger still:
  `{python} f"{PRB['scalar_residual']['per_seed_mean'][0]:.1%}"` and `{python} f"{PRB['scalar_residual']['per_seed_mean'][1]:.1%}"`
  of the pressure prediction under a rigid motion on two trained checkpoints, against
  `{python} f"{PRB['scalar_vs_fp32_unrotated']['mean_over_seeds']:.1%}"` between bfloat16 and float32 with no motion, and
  `{python} f"{PRF['scalar_residual']['max_over_cars']:.3%}"` at worst in float32 (an ISLA at 192 wide, 256 slices, 1e-3,
  linear routing, raw slice reads, @sec-study-configurations; DrivAerML Surface task, twelve validation cars per
  checkpoint; results/precres_2026-09-18.json). Score and deploy in float32 where the contract matters.
:::

## A rigid motion of the body must move the field with it {#sec-equivariance-centerpiece}

**Rotate and translate the body together with the far-field direction, and the field must rotate and translate with it:
scalars unchanged at the moved points, vectors rotated.** A steady problem with a uniform far field has no preferred origin
and no preferred axes. The geometry's relation to the global directions is all the equations see. A surrogate that reads
raw coordinates has to learn that the dataset's axes are arbitrary, from whatever poses its training set happens
to contain, and a dataset in which every car points along $+x$ cannot teach it that. ISLA never reads a coordinate
(@tbl-contracts), so the property costs it no data.

The contract does not by itself make a model more accurate. A coordinate model can be made exactly pose-invariant another
way, as the next section explains, and on a dataset whose cases all arrive in one pose the two routes see the same inputs.
The book therefore attributes no in-distribution accuracy to equivariance. It scores the contract as a contract: every
standing artifact rescores each checkpoint with every validation case rotated and translated (@sec-pose-contract).

### Equivariant by construction, or invariant by canonicalization {#sec-pose}

**A canonicalizing pipeline, which rotates every case to a frame estimated from its own geometry (@sec-landscape-symmetry,
@fig-landscape-canon), is exact only where that frame exists and is unique. ISLA's equivariance does not need one.** The
frame must also be part of training: a model trained in one exact pose and canonicalized only at inference meets the
estimator's small tilt errors as inputs it never saw. The frame fails in two settings a general PDE surrogate meets:

- a body whose inertia tensor is degenerate, or whose third moments vanish, so an axis or its sign cannot be fixed. A
  distinguished global direction fixes one axis, leaving the roll to the transverse inertia tensor; a problem with none
  ($K = 0$: a body under a scalar load, a heat-conduction or electrostatics problem, the GINOT lug of @sec-lug) takes all
  three axes from the shape, and fails wherever two of its principal moments tie;
- an assembly of parts in mixed orientations, where no single frame canonicalizes every part.

ISLA needs neither a frame estimate nor a global direction. ISLA-DTT builds the cluster forest of its boundary read in a
canonical frame of the boundary (measure-weighted centroid, principal axes signed by their third moments;
@sec-arch-tree-read) only to group cells for speed, so a tie of that frame moves its read by the tree's error, not by the
$O(1)$ jump of a network fed canonical coordinates. The forest also splits the cells by the sign octant of their normals
in that frame, and where a normal's component there is zero but for rounding, rounding decides the octant: on the lug,
where most cells are such, 11% of the cells change octant under a rigid motion, ISLA-DTT's posed forest is another
forest, and its posed error is not its native error (@sec-arch-tree-read). In these
settings the contract separates a working surrogate from one whose error a random orientation multiplies by the factors
of @fig-contract-shifts.

**The contract has a clause for outputs that are components in a frame.** A stress component $\sigma_{12}$ or a
displacement along one of the dataset's axes is not a property of the body alone: it belongs to the body and those axes together.
ISLA predicts the tensor itself and reads the component off it (@sec-isla-heads); the dataset's axes are not among its
inputs (@sec-pose-inputs). The clause binds on PLAID Tensile2d, whose targets are stress components (@sec-tensile2d).

### What ISLA is not given {#sec-pose-inputs}

Every input ISLA takes is a datum of the PDE problem (@sec-isla-inputs lists them), and the axes of the dataset's frame
are not one, so ISLA is not given them, not even as extra global vectors. Rotated with every case they would keep the
algebra covariant, but they are not a datum of the PDE; held fixed, as a dataset stores them, they are the pose of the
training set, and a model given them can learn that pose.

## The answer must not depend on how the boundary was meshed {#sec-discretization-centerpiece}

**The physics does not depend on how a surface was meshed, so a model's answer must not either. Numerical consistency is
the precise form of that requirement.** A CFD mesh is refined where the engineer expected gradients, so the density of
points records the mesher's judgment about where the flow is hard. A model that reads that density borrows a
non-physical input, and the input is gone in a new setting: a different mesher, a point cloud sampled from CAD, a geometry
the training set did not contain.

### Discretization consistency is an acceptance criterion {#sec-principle}

**A change to the architecture is adopted only if the model's prediction converges to one field under refinement, and
to the same field under different sampling laws. In-distribution accuracy alone never justifies a
change.** The goal is an accurate surrogate reached by physically principled means, because the principles carry a model to
problems it was not trained on. Model size buys accuracy, but it does not buy generalization to a new mesher. A different
mesher then differs from the training mesher only by a discretization error that vanishes in the fine-mesh limit. An error
that falls as cells are added is the expected behavior of a consistent model. A different answer under a different sampler
at every count is a defect.

A proposed change answers three questions in order. *Why* does it work, stated as a mechanism? Would a CFD practitioner
accept that mechanism as a statement about the problem rather than about the dataset? Does the model converge to the same
field under a biased and an area-proportional resampling as the count grows? The third question is answered by measurement,
never by one accuracy number: the same checkpoint is scored under several sampling laws at several counts. The same
requirement applies to the law a model was *trained* under. A model trained on an area-proportional draw must score like
its uniform-trained twin on an independent draw (@sec-training-law). A configuration that fails the third question can still
be measured, as an ablation that prices the requirement. It does not become part of ISLA.

### The sampling laws {#sec-sampling-laws}

**Every discretization measurement in this book is a statement about which cells of a boundary mesh a model sees, and with
what weight. Three laws recur, and @fig-sampling-laws draws them on one meshed airfoil.** A boundary arrives as a mesh of $N$
cells, refined where the mesher expected gradients. A training or scoring sample keeps $n$ of them. Each kept cell $i$
has a *measure weight* $w_i$, the area (or length) it stands for: its own area divided by its inclusion probability
$\pi_i$. Such weights are the *Horvitz–Thompson* weights of survey sampling, the importance weights of Monte Carlo
quadrature. With them, a weighted sum over the kept cells is an unbiased estimate of the integral over the whole surface,
whatever the law. The laws differ only in $\pi_i$:

- **Uniform over cells, the native law.** Every cell is kept with probability $n/N$. The kept points inherit the mesh's
  refinement, dense where the mesher was. Every model in the book trains under this law, and the *native mesh* scoring uses
  it.
- **Area-proportional, the uniform point cloud.** $\pi_i$ is proportional to the cell's area, so the kept points spread
  evenly over the surface whatever the mesher did. This is what a uniform point generator on a CAD surface delivers. A
  large cell is likely to be kept and a tiny leading-edge cell rarely is, and every kept cell then stands for the same
  area. The mesher's refinement leaves the sample entirely.
- **A biased draw.** Cells ahead of the median $x$ are kept ten times as often as the rest, independently (Poisson
  sampling), with exact $\pi_i$. It is a stress test: the front is over-sampled, and each rear cell stands for ten times
  the area of a front one.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sampling-laws
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The three sampling laws on one meshed airfoil (a Joukowski section at 6° with a mesher-like refinement at the leading
#|   and trailing edges, 400 cells; the ticks mark the cell boundaries). Top three panels: the cells each law keeps at an
#|   expected 80 of 400, one marker per kept cell with marker area proportional to its measure weight (the length it stands
#|   for). Bottom: the density of kept points along the surface under each law, against the mesh's own cell density (gray
#|   fill) and the level of a sample spread evenly over the surface (dashed). The native law follows the mesh; the bias
#|   piles points onto the front half; the area-proportional law is flat, and its kept cells all stand for the same length. How
#|   to read this: the inclusion rules are the recipe's own (`SubsampleMesh`, `PoissonBiasedSubsampleMesh`); the airfoil and
#|   its mesh are an illustration, not a dataset surface, and the weight range printed under each panel is this mesh's.
#| code-fold: true
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
N, n = 400, 80
s_fine = np.linspace(0, 1, 20001)
rho = 1 + 9 * np.exp(-((s_fine - 0.5) / 0.05) ** 2) + 5 * np.exp(-(s_fine / 0.035) ** 2) + 5 * np.exp(-((s_fine - 1) / 0.035) ** 2)
cdf = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(rho[1:] * np.diff(s_fine))]); cdf /= cdf[-1]
FRAC = np.interp(np.linspace(0, 1, N + 1), cdf, s_fine)
Jm = joukowski(alpha_deg=6.0, n_cells=N, frac=FRAC)
xy, mid, w = Jm["xy"], Jm["mid"], Jm["w"]  # w = cell length, the 1-D measure
s_mid = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(w)])[:-1] + w / 2; s_mid /= w.sum()
def uniform_draw():
    return np.sort(rng.choice(N, n, replace=False)), np.full(N, n / N)
def poisson_draw(wts):  # independent sampling with exact pi, as PoissonBiasedSubsampleMesh
    c = n / wts.sum(); pi = np.minimum(1.0, c * wts); deficit = n - pi.sum()
    if deficit > 0:
        free = pi < 1; pi[free] = np.minimum(1.0, pi[free] * (1 + deficit / pi[free].sum()))
    return np.nonzero(rng.random(N) < pi)[0], pi
x_med = np.median(mid[:, 0])
LAWS = [("native: uniform over cells", INK2, uniform_draw),
        ("area-proportional: the uniform point cloud", GREEN, lambda: poisson_draw(w.copy())),
        ("biased: 10:1 front to back", "#b5179e", lambda: poisson_draw(np.where(mid[:, 0] < x_med, 10.0, 1.0)))]
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8.0, 9.2))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(4, 1, height_ratios=[0.62, 0.62, 0.62, 1.0], hspace=0.42)
axes = [fig.add_subplot(gs[i, 0]) for i in range(3)]
densities = []
for ax, (name, col, draw) in zip(axes, LAWS):
    idx, pi = draw(); wt = w[idx] / pi[idx]; rel = wt / wt.min()
    ax.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
    for k in range(N):
        p = xy[k]; d = Jm["nrm"][k]
        ax.plot([p[0], p[0] + 0.05 * d[0]], [p[1], p[1] + 0.05 * d[1]], color=MUTED, lw=0.5, zorder=0)
    ax.scatter(mid[idx, 0], mid[idx, 1], s=14.0 * rel / rel.mean(), c=col, alpha=0.85, zorder=3, lw=0)
    clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.3, 2.3); ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 0.62)
    ax.set_title(name, color=col, fontsize=10)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.04, f"{len(idx)} of {N} cells kept; measure weights span {wt.max() / wt.min():.0f}x", transform=ax.transAxes,
            fontsize=8.5, color=INK2, va="top", ha="center", path_effects=halo())
    if name.startswith("biased"):
        ax.axvline(x_med, color=col, lw=0.8, ls=":", zorder=2)
        ax.text(x_med + 0.05, 0.5, "median x: ten times the rate to the left", color=col, fontsize=8, ha="left", va="center")
    bw = 0.02; grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
    densities.append((name, col, np.array([np.sum(np.exp(-0.5 * ((g - s_mid[idx]) / bw) ** 2)) for g in grid]) / (bw * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)) / w.sum()))
axd = fig.add_subplot(gs[3, 0]); grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
mesh_dens = np.interp(grid, s_mid, 1 / (w / w.sum()) / N)
axd.fill_between(grid, 0, mesh_dens / mesh_dens.mean() * (n / w.sum()), color=GRID, zorder=0, label="the mesh itself (scaled to n cells)")
for name, col, dens in densities:
    axd.plot(grid, dens, color=col, lw=1.8, zorder=3, label=name.split(":")[0])
axd.axhline(n / w.sum(), color=INK2, lw=0.8, ls="--", zorder=2, label="spread evenly (n ÷ perimeter)")
for s_, lab in ((0.0, "trailing edge"), (0.5, "leading edge"), (1.0, "trailing edge")):
    axd.axvline(s_, color=BASELINE, lw=0.8)
    axd.text(s_, 1.01, lab, ha={0.0: "left", 0.5: "center", 1.0: "right"}[s_], va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=MUTED, transform=axd.get_xaxis_transform())
axd.set_xlabel("position along the surface [fraction of arclength]")
axd.set_ylabel("kept points per unit\nsurface length [1/chord]")
axd.set_xlim(0, 1); axd.set_ylim(0, 1.08 * max(d.max() for _, _, d in densities)); axd.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8.5)
plt.show()
```

In symbols, the laws differ in one place. For a field $f$ on the boundary $\Gamma$ and a kept set $\mathcal K$,

$$
\int_\Gamma f \, dA \;\approx\; \sum_{i \in \mathcal K} w_i\, f(x_i), \qquad w_i \equiv \frac{A_i}{\pi_i},
$$ {#eq-ht}

where $A_i$ is cell $i$'s area and $\pi_i$ its inclusion probability. The estimate is unbiased under every law. Its variance
depends on the law, and it shrinks as $n$ grows. Every slice sum inside ISLA (routing mass, anchors, pooled states) is of this
form (@sec-isla-quadrature). Under a change of law, then, ISLA sees the same integrals with a different quadrature error, and
the error vanishes in the limit. A model that averages the kept points as if each stood for the same area sees a different
point cloud under each law, and nothing in it converges to a law-free answer.

### What "consistent" means as a readout {#sec-consistency-bench}

**A model is consistent when its prediction depends on the surface and not on the sample. The readout is the ratio of one
checkpoint's error under two laws, and its convergence toward one as the count grows.** A ratio of exactly one at every count
is not required: the quadrature behind @eq-ht has a variance, and a measure weight that spans decades makes that variance
large at small $n$. What the criterion requires is that the ratio approaches one as the count grows, under every law. A
ratio that stays at a fixed level above one, or a trained function that is right only on the law it was fitted on, is what
the criterion rejects. ISLA claims exactly this convergent form for discretization. Its exact contracts are the ones in
@tbl-contracts.

The book reads consistency with three instruments. The standing artifacts rescore every checkpoint on a uniform point cloud
(@sec-discretization-evidence). Probes on a smaller ISLA score one checkpoint under the biased law at two counts
(@sec-robustness-density). The training-law swap trains each model twice, once under each law (@sec-training-law).

**The point-cloud protocol tests consistency.** The same checkpoint, trained under the native law, is scored on a sample of
the same surfaces drawn by the area law. Every model sees integrals estimated from a different sample, and only the
measure-weighted estimator sees the same integrals. The area law changes two things a baseline reads: which points it
gets (it moves them off the refined features and onto the flat panels) and, through them, the plain mean on which the
datapipe centers its coordinates. Their error grows by the factors in the bottom panel, on cases they score well on the
native mesh. The probes of @sec-contract-studies separate the two causes.

### Pose: a contract, not an accuracy edge {#sec-pose-contract}

**The posed column measures pose invariance, not accuracy. Against baselines trained with rotation augmentation, ISLA's
exactness still shows: augmentation leaves their posed error above their native error, and ISLA's stays at its own.** A baseline trained on randomly rotated cases learns approximate invariance
from data and pays for it in accuracy. @tbl-pose-200k sets every training and validation car of the DrivAerML Surface task
in its own random pose. The comparison was run on a smaller ISLA than the reference configuration, so it is read as a
mechanism, and the factors it gives are not a standing.

## Where ISLA's contract still bends {#sec-contract-bends}

**An interior prediction point reads its wall distance and direction from the exact closest point of the full-resolution
surface, and the length unit is computed from that surface before the draw, so no draw of the boundary tokens moves
either. What still moves ISLA's error is, for interacting ISLA, the request it is queried with, and for both forms a token budget
below the boundary's own resolution, a different surface, and three float32 steps in the geometry.** Everything else a prediction point reads
(slice states, anchors, routing mass) is a measure-weighted quadrature and moves only by its quadrature error
(@sec-isla-interior). The sections below measure each on trained checkpoints at the reference configuration.

### The interior inputs do not depend on the boundary draw {#sec-exact-geometry-draw}

**The class's wall distance is a function of the surface alone, the same for every draw of the boundary tokens; the
nearest-token form's is a function of the draw.** @fig-nearest-token shows both on the airfoil. The distance to the nearest
kept cell overestimates the true one by up to half the gap between neighboring kept cells (on a surface in three dimensions,
by up to the radius of the largest gap between tokens), and the overestimate depends on where the law put its samples. A
model trained under the native law learns to read the native law's distances. Under the area law, which thins the samples
where the mesher refined and adds them where it did not, its near-wall points read distances from a distribution it has not
seen. The exact distance is the blue line at one, whatever the draw (`test_builtin_geometry_is_the_surface_s_for_every_draw_of_the_tokens`).
The scaled distance $s_q = d_q / L$ is the same for every draw too, since $L$ is computed from the full-resolution boundary
before the draw (@sec-arch-frame).

```{python}
#| label: fig-nearest-token
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The wall distance of an interior prediction point on the meshed airfoil of @fig-sampling-laws, read from the nearest
#|   sampled boundary token (the nearest-token form) and from the exact closest point of the surface (ISLA). Top: the front of
#|   the airfoil, the kept cells of one native draw (gray squares) and of one area-proportional draw (green diamonds), each an
#|   expected 80 of the 400 cells, and twelve prediction points (aqua) one hundredth of a chord off the wall, each joined to
#|   its nearest kept cell under each draw. Bottom: for prediction points at that distance all around the airfoil, each
#|   distance divided by the exact distance to the surface. How to read this: 1 is the exact wall distance, which ISLA
#|   reads under every draw (blue); the nearest-token distance is always larger, by up to half the gap between neighboring kept
#|   cells, and the two draws give different values at the same point, so a model calibrated on one law's distances reads
#|   another law's as new inputs. The section, its mesh and the draws are an illustration; no model is involved, and the thin
#|   trailing-edge region (the outer 10% of arclength at each end) is left out.
#| code-fold: true
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
fine = joukowski(alpha_deg=6.0, n_cells=8000)
chord = np.ptp(fine["xy"][:, 0])
delta = 0.01 * chord
def nearest(q, pts):
    d = np.linalg.norm(q[:, None, :] - pts[None, :, :], axis=-1)
    return d.min(axis=1), d.argmin(axis=1)
s_f = (np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(fine["w"])])[:-1] + fine["w"] / 2) / fine["w"].sum()
sel = np.nonzero((s_f > 0.1) & (s_f < 0.9))[0][::12]
Q = fine["mid"][sel] + delta * fine["nrm"][sel]
d_exact, _ = nearest(Q, fine["mid"])
draw_nat = rng.choice(N, n, replace=False)
pi_a = np.minimum(1.0, n * w / w.sum()); draw_area = np.nonzero(rng.random(N) < pi_a)[0]
x0 = fine["mid"][:, 0].min()
front = np.nonzero((s_f > 0.38) & (s_f < 0.62))[0]
show = front[np.linspace(0, len(front) - 1, 12).astype(int)]
Qs = fine["mid"][show] + delta * fine["nrm"][show]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8.0, 7.4), gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1.25, 1.0], hspace=0.3))
ax = axs[0]
ax.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=BASELINE, lw=1.2, zorder=1)
for dr, col in ((draw_nat, INK2), (draw_area, GREEN)):
    _, j = nearest(Qs, mid[dr])
    for q, c in zip(Qs, mid[dr][j]):
        ax.plot([q[0], c[0]], [q[1], c[1]], color=col, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
ax.plot(mid[draw_nat, 0], mid[draw_nat, 1], "s", ms=5, color=INK2, ls="none", zorder=3, label="kept cell, native draw")
ax.plot(mid[draw_area, 0], mid[draw_area, 1], "D", ms=5.5, color=GREEN, mfc="white", mew=1.4, ls="none", zorder=3, label="kept cell, area-proportional draw")
ax.plot(Qs[:, 0], Qs[:, 1], "o", ms=4.5, color=AQUA, zorder=4, label="prediction point, 0.01 chord off the wall")
ax.set_xlim(x0 - 0.03 * chord, x0 + 0.33 * chord); ax.set_ylim(-0.085 * chord, 0.095 * chord); map_axes(ax)
ax.set_xlabel(f"x [section units; chord {chord:.1f}]"); ax.set_ylabel("y [section units]")
ax.set_title("the front of the airfoil: each prediction point joined to its nearest kept cell under each draw", fontsize=9.5)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8, frameon=True, facecolor="white", edgecolor=BASELINE)
ax = axs[1]
for dr, col, lab in ((draw_nat, INK2, "nearest token, native draw"), (draw_area, GREEN, "nearest token, area-proportional draw")):
    d_s, _ = nearest(Q, mid[dr])
    ax.plot(s_f[sel], d_s / d_exact, color=col, lw=1.5, label=lab)
ax.axhline(1, color=BLUE, lw=2.2, label="exact closest point (ISLA), every draw")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_yticks([1, 2, 5, 10]); ax.set_yticklabels(["1", "2", "5", "10"]); ax.yaxis.set_minor_locator(NullLocator())
ax.axvline(0.5, color=BASELINE, lw=0.8); ax.text(0.5, 0.97, "leading edge", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=8, color=MUTED, transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(), path_effects=halo())
ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_xlabel("position of the prediction point along the surface [fraction of arclength from the trailing edge]")
ax.set_ylabel("read ÷ exact\nwall distance [–]"); ax.set_ylim(0.9, 25); ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8.5)
plt.show()
```

### Re-meshing the boundary {#sec-remesh-measured}

```{python}
#| label: para-remesh-lede
#| output: asis
EXACT = [(RA, "r090eag_af_isla", v) for v in ("refine2", "refine4", "refine31")] + [(RV, "r090_vol_isla", v) for v in ("tok100k", "tok400k", "subdiv4")]
exact_dev = max(abs(rm(n, a, v, f) - 1) for n, a, v in EXACT for f, _ in QF)
budget = [rm(RA, "r090eag_af_isla", f"tok{k}", "pressure_l2") for k in (600, 400, 200)]
n_af = R.load(P, RA)["runs"]["r090eag_af_isla_seed42"]["native_inputs"]["n_cells"]["median"]
stl = [rm(RV, "r090_vol_isla", "stl", f) for f, _ in QF]
band = R.md_table(P, "RESULTS.md", "Analyses beside")
far_band = [r for r in band if r["points"].startswith("≥")][0]
far_dev = max(abs(R.num(far_band[c], k) - 1) for c in ("pressure r", "velocity r", "nut r") for k in (0, 1))
near_L = R.num(far_band["points"])
SO = BA["stl_offset"]
print(f"**Re-mesh the boundary exactly, and ISLA's error does not move: splitting every panel of the airfoil, "
      f"subdividing every cell of the car, or changing the number of tokens drawn from the car leaves it within "
      f"{exact_dev:.1%} of native on every field (@tbl-remesh).** This is the discretization contract measured on trained "
      "checkpoints at the reference configuration. The slice reads are measure-weighted quadratures, and the length unit and "
      "the prediction points' geometry are computed from the full-resolution boundary, so an exact re-meshing changes only the "
      "quadrature error. Two things do move the error, and neither is an exact re-meshing. A token budget below the "
      f"boundary's own cell count (a median of {n_af:,.0f} panels on the airfoil) raises the AirfRANS pressure error "
      f"{min(budget):.2f}-fold to {max(budget):.2f}-fold as the budget falls from 600 to 200 tokens; at 400 tokens the loss is "
      "the variance of the draw: on seed 42, two draws of that budget differ from each other more than either differs from "
      "native. "
      "A different surface is a different "
      f"input: the watertight STL of the car in place of its CFD wall raises the DrivAerML Volume error {min(stl):.2f}-fold to "
      f"{max(stl):.2f}-fold, almost all of it within {near_L:g} L of the wall; farther out the error moves by at most "
      f"{far_dev:.1%}. The two surfaces differ by a median of {sci(SO['median_L'])} L, about {SO['median_L'] / 1e-6:.0f} times the "
      "softening of the distance channel, and that offset is the whole wall distance of the prediction points that lie on the "
      "CFD wall. That the offset causes the near-wall rise fits these numbers but was not tested (an analysis after the "
      "registered reading; scratch/isla-probes090-2026-10-21/diag_stl/STL_OFFSET.md, read into "
      "results/campaigns_2026-10-22/book_A/book_a.json).")
```

```{python}
#| label: cell-tbl-remesh
#| output: asis
TOK0 = int(R.load(P, RV)["runs"]["r090_vol_isla_seed42"]["native_inputs"]["tokens"]["median"])
def what(v):
    """A re-meshing variant of PROBES-090 as (description, kind)."""
    if v.startswith("refine"):
        return ({"refine2": "every panel split in two", "refine4": "every panel split in four",
                 "refine31": "panels split more finely toward the front"}[v], "exact")
    if v.startswith("tok"):
        k = int(v[3:-1]) * 1000 if v.endswith("k") else int(v[3:])
        return (f"{k:,} tokens drawn in the model" + (f" (native {TOK0:,})" if v.endswith("k") else ""), "exact" if v.endswith("k") else "budget")
    if v.startswith("decim"):
        return (f"a coarser polyline of {int(v[5:]):,} segments", "new surface")
    if v.startswith("redraw"):
        return (f"another draw at the native budget, systematic start {int(v[8:]) / 100:g}", "draw floor")
    return {"subdiv4": ("every cell subdivided into four", "exact"), "stl": ("the watertight STL in place of the CFD wall", "new surface")}[v]
GROUPS = ((RA, "r090eag_af_isla", "AirfRANS airfoil, ISLA", ("refine2", "refine4", "refine31", "tok800", "tok600", "tok400", "tok200", "decim400", "decim200")),
          (RD, "r090eag_af_dtt", "AirfRANS airfoil, ISLA-DTT", ("refine2", "refine4", "refine31")),
          (RV, "r090_vol_isla", "DrivAerML Volume car, ISLA", ("tok100k", "tok400k", "subdiv4", "redraw_u0", "redraw_u25", "stl")))
out = ["| boundary and model | variant | kind | pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity |", "|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|"]
for name, arm, lab, variants in GROUPS:
    for v in variants:
        d, kind = what(v)
        out.append(f"| {lab} | {d} | {kind} | " + " | ".join(f"{rm(name, arm, v, f):.4f}" if v in ("refine2", "refine4", "refine31", "tok100k", "tok400k", "subdiv4", "redraw_u0", "redraw_u25") else S.fmt_ratio(rm(name, arm, v, f)) for f, _ in QF) + " |")
print("\n".join(out))
nc = lambda name, run: R.load(P, name)["runs"][run]["n_cases"]
print("\n: Re-meshing the boundary of trained checkpoints: each arm's error with the changed boundary over its error with the "
      "native one, seed-mean ratio over two seeds, float32, eager, final checkpoints; "
      f"{nc(RA, 'r090eag_af_isla_seed42')} AirfRANS test cases and {nc(RV, 'r090_vol_isla_seed42')} DrivAerML Volume validation "
      "cars. *exact*: the same surface, meshed or drawn differently; *budget*: fewer tokens than the airfoil has panels; "
      "*new surface*: a different geometry, a test of robustness rather than of invariance; *draw floor*: a second draw at the "
      "native budget, the noise against which the car's rows are read. The AirfRANS checkpoints are "
      + PROBE_CKPT + ". How to read this: 1 is no change; a ratio compares a "
      "checkpoint with itself. Data: " + "; ".join(R.source(P, n) for n in (RA, RV)) + ". {#tbl-remesh}")
```

### The other prediction points of a request {#sec-query-population}

```{python}
#| label: para-query-lede
#| output: asis
af = lambda m: [qr(QA, AF_I, m, f) for f, _ in QF]
SUBS = sorted((m for m in R.load(P, QA)[AF_I[0]]["ratio_to_native_h"] if m.startswith("sub")), key=lambda m: -int(m[3:]))
small = [x for m in SUBS for x in af(m)]
vol_small = [qr(QV, VOL, m, f) for m in SUBS for f, _ in QF]
vol_pv = max(abs(qr(QV, VOL, m, f) - 1) for m in ("half", "chunks4") for f in ("pressure_l2", "velocity_l2"))
az_mild = max(abs(qr(QZ, AZ, m, f) - 1) for m in ("half", "chunks4", "far") for f, _ in QF)
az_one = [qr(QZ, AZ, "sub1", f) for f, _ in QF]
dtt_dev = max(abs(v - 1) for r in AF_D for m in R.load(P, QA)[r]["ratio_to_native_h"].values() for v in m.values())
print("**Interacting ISLA's prediction at a point depends on the other points of the request, and no knob makes that "
      "dependence vanish: on the AirfRANS interior task, sending the same points in four chunks raises the error "
      f"{min(af('chunks4')):.2f}-fold to {max(af('chunks4')):.2f}-fold, and queries of at most {int(SUBS[0][3:]):,} points "
      f"raise it {min(small):.1f}-fold to {max(small):.0f}-fold (@tbl-query-population).** Every prediction point is a token "
      "that writes into the slices with a share of the routing mass (@sec-isla-interior), so the slice states it reads back are "
      "integrals over the whole request. The size of the effect depends on the task. On the DrivAerML Volume task, chunking and "
      f"halving the request stay within {vol_pv:.1%} on pressure and velocity, while small queries cost {min(vol_small):.1f}-fold "
      f"to {max(vol_small):.0f}-fold. On AeroZoo's `full` split, chunking, halving and far-field companions move the error by "
      f"at most {az_mild:.0%}, and single points cost {min(az_one):.1f}-fold to {max(az_one):.1f}-fold. ISLA-DTT's prediction "
      f"points are read-only, and on AirfRANS its error moves by at most {sci(dtt_dev)} in every mode, float32 roundoff "
      "(@sec-arch-passive-decoder). Interacting ISLA is therefore queried with the whole field's prediction points at once, "
      "drawn by the law it was trained on; ISLA-DTT needs no such condition.")
```

### Ties in the geometry {#sec-medial-ties}

**Exact geometry has no ties between samples, and in the geometry the standings trained with three of its steps turned
on float32 rounding: the closest feature of a point equally far from two, the sign of the distance at a fold of the
surface, and which cells the token draw keeps. The class's geometry makes the first two functions of the mesh alone and
the third independent of the compute precision.** The tie takes the least-norm direction of the tied features, the sign
comes from the generalized winding number, and the draw is computed in float64 in the boundary's canonical frame
(@sec-arch-interior-geometry, @sec-arch-boundary-draw). Below, each step is measured first as the standings' checkpoints
saw it, then with the class's rule (@sec-standing-geometry).

```{python}
#| label: para-ties
#| output: asis
L_, T_ = ST["lug"], ST["tensile2d"]
pn = lambda st, f: [p / n for p, n in zip(st.seeds("ISLA", f, "posed"), st.seeds("ISLA", f, "native"))]
t_pn = [x for f in T_.ds.headline for x in pn(T_, f)]
LT = BA["lug_ties"]
print(f"On PLAID Tensile2d, ISLA's rotated-and-translated error is {min(t_pn):.4f} to {max(t_pn):.4f} times its native error "
      f"over its {S._COUNT[T_.n_seeds('ISLA')]} seeds and {S._COUNT[len(T_.ds.headline)]} headline fields ({T_.source}). On the GINOT "
      f"bracket lug it is {' and '.join(f'{x:.2f}' for x in pn(L_, 'von_mises_l2'))} times native on the two seeds "
      f"({L_.source}).\n")
print(S.in_flight_callout({"what": L_.in_flight["what"].replace("ISLA", "ISLA on the GINOT bracket lug", 1),
                           "replacement": L_.in_flight["replacement"]} if L_.in_flight else None))
print("A prediction point's direction is the unit gradient of its distance to the surface. On the *medial surface*, the set of "
      "points with two or more closest surface features, that gradient is not defined: a node on a thin plate's mid-thickness "
      "plane is equally far from the top and the bottom face. In the geometry the standings trained with, the closest-feature "
      "search keeps the first feature it meets, so the order of the mesh's vertices decides the direction there. On the lug, a "
      "geometry-only test of that geometry that reverses the "
      f"winding of every cell finds {LT['nodes']:,} interior nodes in {LT['n_cases']} test cases ({LT['interior_fraction']:.1%} "
      f"of the interior, {LT['per_case_min']} to {LT['per_case_max']} per case) whose direction changes, by up to $\\pi$, while "
      f"their distance does not ({R.source('attrib090', 'RESULTS.md')}, section 4). A rotation and translation rounds the "
      "coordinates differently and can pick the other feature at the same nodes, and because the prediction points join the "
      "encoder as tokens, the change spreads to the slices.\n")
TX = R.load("tie_exp", "read/results.json")
TF = lambda run, f: TX["F"][f"F_code_{run}:{f}"]
tie_pn = [TX["lug"]["posed"]["tie"][s]["von_mises_l2"] / TX["lug"]["native"]["tie"][s]["von_mises_l2"] for s in ("42", "43")]
fl_tie = [TF(f"tie2_tie_lug_isla_seed{s}", "von_mises")["median"] for s in (42, 43)]
fl_b = [TF(f"cmpaf_fix_r090eag_lug_isla_seed{s}", "von_mises")["median"] for s in (42, 43)]
fl_t2d = max(v["max"] for k, v in TX["F"].items() if k.startswith("F_code_tie2_tie_t2dz"))
assert fl_t2d == 0
NL, NT = TX["lug"]["N"]["von_mises_l2"], TX["t2d"]["N"]["displacement_l2"]
print(f"**With the class's tie rule the lug's posed excess falls to {100 * TX['lug']['P']['von_mises_l2']['ratio']:.1f}% of the "
      "standing's, at no native cost.** ISLA trained with the least-norm tie "
      "direction on the lug and on Tensile2d, two seeds each, from the standing's snapshot and recipe with only the geometry "
      f"changed, and scored as the standing was, reads posed ÷ native {1 + TX['lug']['P']['von_mises_l2']['e_TIE']:.4f} on the "
      f"lug's von Mises stress ({' and '.join(f'{x:.4f}' for x in tie_pn)} per seed), against "
      f"{1 + TX['lug']['P']['von_mises_l2']['e_B']:.3f} for the standing's checkpoints (ratios of seed means; the excess is posed "
      "÷ native minus one). Its native error is "
      f"{NL['r']:.3f} times the lug standing's, and {NT['r']:.3f} times that of seeds 42 and 43 of the four-seed Tensile2d "
      "standing on displacement (ratios of seed means), and the "
      f"registered test reads both as \"{NL['verdict']}\"; on Tensile2d, whose seeds are far apart, its band is "
      f"±{2 * NT['sigma']:.2f} in the logarithm, so there it rules out only a large cost. Under a reversal of every cell's winding "
      "with the matching negation of the weights, the median residual of the trained models' prediction is "
      f"{' and '.join(f'{x:.2e}' for x in fl_tie)} on the lug, float32 rounding, against {' and '.join(f'{x:.2e}' for x in fl_b)} "
      f"for the standing's, and exactly {fl_t2d:.0f} on Tensile2d, which the registered test reads as \"{TX['F_verdict']}\". "
      "The registered reading of the pose is that \""
      f"{TX['lug']['P']['von_mises_l2']['verdict']}\" ({R.source('tie_exp', 'read/results.json')}; @sec-lug-ties).\n")
F32 = R.md_table("az_diag", "f32floor/README.md", "3. Results")
F32_HI = [r for r in F32 if r["run"] != "controls"]           # the cases chosen for their large float32 error
flips = [int(r["sign flips (CPU)"]) for r in F32_HI if int(r["sign flips (CPU)"]) > 0]
cells = [int(x.replace(",", "")) for r in F32_HI for x in re.findall(r"\d[\d,]*", r["cells D32≠D64"])]
N_PTS = int(re.search(r"\(of ([\d,]+)\)", R.load("az_diag", "f32floor/README.md")).group(1).replace(",", ""))
print("In the geometry the standings trained with, at a fold of the surface, where cells meet back to back, the pseudo-normal that signs the distance cancels exactly, "
      "so roundoff picks the sign; the sign is ill-posed there in exact arithmetic, and float64 would make it reproducible "
      "without making it right. The third step is the token draw: it orders the cells along a quantized Morton curve, "
      "and rounding moves cells across the quantization. On AeroZoo cases chosen for their large float32 error, "
      f"up to {max(flips):,} of {N_PTS:,} prediction points per case flip the sign of their wall distance between float32 and "
      f"float64, on {len(flips)} of the {len(F32_HI)} cases, and {min(cells)} to {max(cells):,} of the {N_PTS:,} drawn boundary "
      "cells change "
      f"({R.source('az_diag', 'f32floor/README.md')}). On every one of those cases, computing the geometry in float64 removes "
      "nearly all of the difference between ISLA's float32 and float64 predictions, and computing the network's blocks in "
      "float64 removes none of it.\n")
FS = R.load("fold_sign", "f32floor_tables.md")
fs_cases = int(re.search(r"cases: (\d+) of \d+", FS).group(1))
assert re.search(r"R1: N_flip outside the band summed over cases = 0; in the band = 0", FS)
TD = R.md_table("token_draw", "DESIGN.md", "2. Measurement")
assert all(int(r["precision base / v1 / v2"].split("/")[-1]) == 0 for r in TD)
cut = [R.num(r["v2 cut"]) for r in TD if "degenerate" not in r["case (family)"]]
n_deg = sum("degenerate" in r["case (family)"] for r in TD)
print(f"With the class's winding-number sign, the registered repeat of that comparison on {fs_cases} AeroZoo `full` cases finds "
      "no prediction point whose sign changes between float32 and float64 "
      f"({R.source('fold_sign', 'f32floor_tables.md')}). The class's draw keeps the same cells at both precisions on all {len(TD)} "
      "AeroZoo and DrivAerML cases measured, and under a rotation with a translation its canonical frame cuts the cells that "
      f"change {min(cut):g} to {max(cut):g} times on the {len(cut)} cases whose frame is well defined; on the {n_deg} whose "
      "principal moments nearly tie it cuts none, and what is left elsewhere is float32 rounding of the posed coordinates "
      f"across the grid lines of the Morton code ({R.source('token_draw', 'DESIGN.md')}, section 2).")
```

::: {.callout-note title="In flight"}
The posed ÷ native ratios of the standings in this section come from checkpoints trained with the geometry of
@sec-standing-geometry, whose ties follow the order of the search. Standings trained with the class's geometry replace
them, and the ledger (@sec-ledger) tracks them.
:::

## Studies on a smaller ISLA {#sec-contract-studies}

**Three probes on a smaller ISLA measure what the standing cannot: how the shift falls with the sample count,
what happens when the training law changes, and where inside the network the dependence on the sample lives.** Each caption has
the study tag of @sec-study-configurations. They are read for slopes and mechanisms, and their errors are never a standing.
The probes perturb different things. The biased draw changes the scored sample, and with it the plain mean on which the
baselines' coordinates are centered. The training-law swap changes the sample a model is fitted on and scores every
checkpoint on one native draw. The territory probe looks inside the network under the biased draw.

### The biased draw at two counts {#sec-robustness-density}

**Under a 10:1 biased draw, ISLA's error moves by a residual that shrinks as the count doubles. The baselines' errors grow
by factors.** This is the convergence the criterion of @sec-principle asks for. Each checkpoint is scored on its
validation surfaces under an independent native draw and under the biased draw of @sec-sampling-laws, both with exact
measure weights, and the readout is biased ÷ native.

```{python}
#| label: cell-tbl-density
#| output: asis
CR = J("consistency_r1_2026-09-23.json")["arms"]; TC = J("trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json"); TW = J("trainarea_reduction_2026-09-20.json")
WB = J("wingbench_200k_reduction_2026-09-19.json")["arms"]
rows = [("DrivAerML Surface task", "100,000", "ISLA", CR["isla_r1_dr435_100k"]["density_factor"]),
        ("DrivAerML Surface task", "200,000", "ISLA", CR["isla_r1_dr435_200k"]["density_factor"]),
        ("DrivAerML Surface task", "100,000", "GeoTransolver", TC["arms"]["gt_unit_uniform"]["density_factor"]),
        ("DrivAerML Surface task", "100,000", "Transolver", TC["arms"]["transolver_unit_uniform"]["density_factor"]),
        ("HiLiftAeroML, 35 training cases", "200,000", "ISLA", CR["isla_r1_hl35_200k"]["density_factor"]),
        ("HiLiftAeroML, 35 training cases", "200,000", "GeoTransolver", WB["gt_unit_lr3e3"]["density_factor"]),
        ("HiLiftAeroML, 35 training cases", "200,000", "Transolver", WB["transolver_unit"]["density_factor"])]
out = "| task | cells per draw | architecture | biased ÷ native draw |\n|---|---:|---|---:|\n"
out += "".join(f"| {a} | {b} | {c} | {S.fmt_ratio(r)} |\n" for a, b, c, r in rows)
print(out)
print(": Surface pressure error under the 10:1 biased draw divided by the same checkpoint's error under an independent native "
      "draw, float32, seed means over two seeds, 48 validation cars and 180 validation wings. GeoTransolver and Transolver are "
      "256 wide. How to read this: 1 is a prediction that depends on the surface only; the ISLA rows at two counts on the "
      "same checkpoint show the residual falling as the sample grows; the table does not show the errors themselves. " + tag(384, 256, "5e-4")
      + " Data: results/consistency_r1_2026-09-23.json; results/trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json; "
        "results/wingbench_200k_reduction_2026-09-19.json. {#tbl-density}")
```

```{python}
#| label: para-density-mechanism
#| output: asis
ts = TC["arms"]["transolver_unit_uniform"]["per_seed"]
tseeds = [v["biased"] / v["unif"] for v in ts.values()]
MW = J("mwaw_2026-09-11.json")["runs"]
mw = {a: (MW[k]["probe_sfaw"]["ratio_mean"], MW[k]["probe_sfht"]["ratio_mean"]) for a, k in
      (("GeoTransolver", "mwaw_dr_gt_unit_lr1e3"), ("Transolver", "mwaw_dr_transolver_unit_lr3e3"))}
print(f"Transolver's two DrivAerML seeds read {S.fmt_ratio(min(tseeds))} and {S.fmt_ratio(max(tseeds))} "
      "(results/trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json), a factor of two apart, so its row is a coarse number.\n\n"
      "**For the baselines, the mechanism is the center.** The recipe's datapipe centers each case's coordinates on the plain "
      "mean of the cells it receives, and the probe applies that centering after the draw, as the pipeline would to a mesh "
      "delivered with this density. A biased draw moves the plain mean toward the over-sampled front, and every coordinate "
      "GeoTransolver and Transolver see moves with it (@sec-isla-frame shows the same shift on the airfoil). A control isolates "
      "it: GeoTransolver and Transolver with ISLA's measure-weighted pooling, centered on the area-weighted mean of the drawn "
      f"cells, still move by {S.fmt_ratio(mw['GeoTransolver'][0])} and {S.fmt_ratio(mw['Transolver'][0])} under the bias, and "
      f"centered on the Horvitz–Thompson estimate of the centroid, by {S.fmt_ratio(mw['GeoTransolver'][1])} and "
      f"{S.fmt_ratio(mw['Transolver'][1])} (DrivAerML Surface task, 48 validation cars, 10,000 cells, two seeds; "
      "results/mwaw_2026-09-11.json). ISLA's learned maps use no center (ISLA-DTT's forest uses one only to group cells for speed, @sec-arch-modes): positions enter as differences to anchors, which are "
      "measure-weighted means and move only by their quadrature error. That error is the residual in the ISLA rows, and it "
      "falls as the count grows, as the variance of @eq-ht requires.")
```

### The law the training sample is drawn by {#sec-training-law}

**A GeoTransolver or Transolver checkpoint is accurate on the sampling law it was trained under and on no other. ISLA's
trained function depends on the law weakly: within the preregistered band on the wings, outside it on the cars.** Changing the draw at inference is half of the question. The other half is
the one a practitioner meets when a surrogate trained on one mesher's output receives a mesh from another. Each
architecture is trained twice, under the native law and under the area-proportional law, and both checkpoints are scored on
one independent native draw (@fig-training-law).

```{python}
#| label: fig-training-law

#|   native law and the open marker the same configuration trained under the area-proportional law; both are scored on one

#|   435 training cars, 48 validation cars, 100,000 cells per case. GeoTransolver and Transolver are 256 wide. How to read
#|   this: the filled marker sits left of the open one; two markers at one height mean the trained function does not depend on the law its training sample was drawn

        us = [s["unif"] for s in arms[f"{m}_uniform"]["per_seed"].values()]; as_ = [s["unif"] for s in arms[f"{m}_area"]["per_seed"].values()]
        kw = series_kwargs(key)
        ax.plot([k - 0.08, k + 0.08], [u, a], color=kw["color"], lw=1.6, zorder=2)
        ax.plot([k - 0.08], [u], marker=kw["marker"], color=kw["color"], mfc=kw["color"], mec=kw["color"], ls="none", ms=9, zorder=4)
        ax.plot([k + 0.08], [a], marker=kw["marker"], color=kw["color"], mfc="none", mec=kw["color"], mew=1.8, ls="none", ms=9, zorder=4)
        ax.plot([k - 0.27, k - 0.21], us, ls="none", marker="o", color=kw["color"], ms=3.2, zorder=5)
        ax.plot([k + 0.21, k + 0.27], as_, ls="none", marker="o", mfc="white", color=kw["color"], ms=3.2, zorder=5)
        ax.text(k + 0.34, (u * a) ** 0.5, f"×{S.fmt_ratio(a / u)}", color=kw["color"], fontsize=9.5, va="center", path_effects=halo())
    ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xticks([0, 1, 2]); ax.set_xticklabels([a_[0] for a_ in ARMS])
    ax.set_yticks([0.04, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5]); ax.set_yticklabels(["0.04", "0.1", "0.2", "0.5"]); ax.yaxis.set_minor_locator(NullLocator())
    ax.set_ylim(0.035, 0.6); ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 2.7); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9.5); ax.set_ylabel("surface pressure\nrelative L2 error [–]")
axs[0].text(0.02, 0.95, "filled: trained under the native law\nopen: trained under the area-proportional law", transform=axs[0].transAxes,
            fontsize=8.5, color=INK2, va="top")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: cell-tbl-consistency-40k
#| output: asis
def paired(arms, m):
    su = arms[f"{m}_uniform"]["per_seed"]; sa = arms[f"{m}_area"]["per_seed"]
    return [sa[s]["unif"] / su[s]["unif"] for s in su]
out = "| architecture | HiLiftAeroML, 35 training cases | DrivAerML Surface task, 435 training cars |\n|---|---:|---:|\n"
for label, m, _ in ARMS:
    pw, pc = paired(W, m), paired(C, m)
    out += (f"| {label} | {S.fmt_ratio(TW['verdict'][f'{m}_area_over_uniform_unif'])} ({' / '.join(S.fmt_ratio(x) for x in pw)}) | "
            f"{S.fmt_ratio(TC['verdict'][f'{m}_area_over_uniform_unif'])} ({' / '.join(S.fmt_ratio(x) for x in pc)}) |\n")
print(out)
print(": The training-law ratio: the error of the checkpoint trained under the area-proportional law divided by that of the "
      "same configuration trained under the native law, both scored on one independent native draw (float32, seed means; the "
      "seed-paired ratios in parentheses). How to read this: 1 means the trained function does not depend on the law; the "
      "errors themselves are in @fig-training-law. "
      + tag(192, 256, "1e-3", linear=True) + " Data: results/trainarea_reduction_2026-09-20.json; "
        "results/trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json. {#tbl-consistency-40k}")
```

```{python}
#| label: para-training-law-verdict
#| output: asis
print(f"The registered verdicts read the ISLA rows as they are: on the wings the ratio is "
      f"{S.fmt_ratio(TW['verdict']['isla_area_over_uniform_unif'])}, a null; on the cars it is "
      f"{S.fmt_ratio(TC['verdict']['isla_area_over_uniform_unif'])}, outside the 5% band set before the test, and the "
      "registered reading is that ISLA's indifference to the training law is not general. The baselines' factors are "
      f"{S.fmt_ratio(min(TW['verdict'][f'{m}_area_over_uniform_unif'] for m in ('gt_unit', 'transolver_unit')))} and more.")
```

This probe scores every checkpoint on one native draw, so the scored points and their center are the same for both
checkpoints of a model. What differs is the sample each was fitted on. The baselines' slice aggregates are averages over
the kept points, counted once each, so the trained function absorbs the point pattern it was fitted on. ISLA's aggregates
are measure-weighted integrals, the same under any law whose weights come with the sample. The baselines' dependence is larger on the cars than on
the wings, although the cars' cell areas spread less; the cell-area spread alone does not explain the difference
(@sec-open-questions).

### Where the slices sit {#sec-territories}

```{python}
#| label: para-territory-lede
#| output: asis
TT = J("territory_r1_2026-09-23.json")["models"]; TTW = J("territory_wings_r1_2026-09-23.json")["models"]; TT200 = J("territory_r1_200k_2026-09-23.json")["models"]
I, G = TT["ISLA"]["summary"], TT["GeoTransolver"]["summary"]
IW, GW = TTW["ISLA"]["summary"], TTW["GeoTransolver"]["summary"]
print("**Consistency of the output implies consistency of the internal partition, and the partition can be looked at: "
      "GeoTransolver's slices follow the points, and ISLA's stay on the surface.** Under the 10:1 biased draw, GeoTransolver's "
      f"slice mean positions move by {G['displacement_median']:.2f} of the car's RMS radius and ISLA's anchors by "
      f"{I['displacement_median']:.2f}; on the wings, {GW['displacement_median']:.2f} against {IW['displacement_median']:.3f}. "
      "The probe records each token's *dominant slice* (the slice that gives it the largest weight) in every block, under two "
      "independent native draws and under the biased draw. It matches every token of one draw to its nearest token in another "
      "and counts how often the dominant slice agrees. Two native draws set the *resampling floor*, below one because soft "
      "slice boundaries move under any resampling. The *bias excess* is how much further the agreement falls when the second "
      "draw is the biased one.")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-territory-maps
```
